title: The three-player combat test behind my AI-assisted browser conquest game
author: DadaQuiTrade
selftext:
I'm building CLAIMED, a shared-map strategy game with AI assistance for implementation and some copy. Players claim countries with regenerating Influence, form small alliances and attack across land borders. This is a real screenshot of the playable beta.

One rule needed a very explicit example. Suppose an attacker sends 30 points against a rival with 20 in a neighboring country. They cancel each other out, leaving the attacker with 10. A third group already has 15 there and wasn't targeted, so that group still leads the country. Removing your chosen rival and taking control are separate outcomes.

The project has an automated test for that exact case, plus checks for land adjacency and alliance permissions. For AI-assisted development, those concrete examples give the implementation a precise expected result. They still don't tell me whether the choices are fun or whether the country panel explains them well. That's what I'm trying to learn from outside players now.

The stack is Next.js and React. Playable here: [https://claimed-world.vercel.app/](https://claimed-world.vercel.app/) . It's an early free beta with English, French and Spanish options. A free account and email verification are required. Optional paid sponsor logos are separate from conquest and don't add combat strength.

If you've used AI to implement strategy-game rules, which edge cases did you make explicit before you trusted the result?
